newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Feared rise in NZ mortgage rates becoming reality.
newsitem.headline: Feared rise in NZ mortgage rates becoming reality.

text.p: The second sharp rise in mortgage rates by a major New Zealand lender in two days confirmed the worst fears of many economic observers on Thursday as most home loan rates now look set to surge above 10 percent.
ANZ/Postbank lifted its variable rate to 10.4 percent from 8.95 percent, mirroring a slightly larger jump to 10.5 percent from the same level by its rival Countrywide Bank on Wednesday.

The uptrend means retail borrowers will start to carry some of the pain seen in New Zealand's wholesale money markets in recent weeks when a sharp fall in the value of the kiwi dollar has spurred a compensatory jump in 90-day bank bill rates.

Some manufacturers say they believe high real lending rates are also damaging competitiveness and business confidence, while opposition politicians joined in by criticising the imbalance between real rates and New Zealand's benign inflation outlook.
Other banks said they would inevitably be joining in the move to higher mortgages, even if they may wait a short while.
One lending manager told Reuters on Thursday his bank would announce rises across the board on Friday or next Monday.
"We are reviewing the variable rate now, and it's likely the quantum leap will be very similar to Countrywide's," he said.

Bank of New Zealand, one of the biggest high street banks, has said it will go ahead as planned with a cut to its variable rate to 8.95 percent due on August 4, but will immediately review it. At the same time it is going to raise fixed rates.
Countrywide managing director David Wolfenden told New Zealand TV's One network news on Thursday the rising cost of borrowing may well put New Zealand on the brink of recession.

"It could mean a recessionary environment. Business confidence is down, the retail environment is not performing at all well and we have what really is an untenable situation with rising costs in an economy that is very flat," he said.
The Wellington Manufacturers Association echoed this in a statement attacking the trend towards higher rates and saying it made a recovery in commercial growth much harder.

"The New Zealand economy has lost its international competitiveness primarily as a result of our exchange rate/interest rate mix and so our added-value sector has had to focus on cost reduction and investment reduction rather than
continuing its necessary journey to world class," it said.

Opposition Labour Party finance spokesman Michael Cullen added his voice to the critics who say economic policy has failed to address a trough in growth which indicators suggest began at the start of this year and has yet to turn upwards.
The government and central bank have meanwhile managed to maintain inflation at low levels -- just 1.1 percent underlying in the June quarter -- as GDP growth has levelled off sharply.

"We have low inflation -- but despite the restructuring of the last 13 years we remain unable to enjoy the benefits of (that) in terms of low interest rates and exchange rates," Cullen said in a statement.

Earlier in the day Finance Minister Bill Birch referred only indirectly to the interest rate situation in a speech to businessmen, when he said the adjustment to the mix of interest and exchange rates seen in recent weeks appeared complete.

Otherwise he urged them to share the government's optimism that growth is around the corner and will take its roots in the lower dollar, increased government spending, healthy export markets, forecast higher commodity prices and lower taxes.
